notes.text: I'm going to start by reading through the mission briefing to get oriented.

I'm working out the plan: test drops at different heights would let me read wind speed and direction at aircraft altitude, along with shear and veer, though the measurements carry some noise. Impact points could reveal drag, and I'm keeping in mind that updrafts from the smoke will affect drops that pass through it. I'm leaning toward running the test drops away from the fire, outside the smoke, to determine

I'm mapping out the wind measurements at each altitude, using the shear and veer to estimate speed and direction at 150 m, 50 m, and 30 m from what I get at 100 m. Next I'm planning to release several test drops at different altitudes, outside the smoke, with varied headings and speeds, and run them in parallel.

I'm working out the wind shear exponent from the measurements at each height. At 100 the wind is 6.2 heading 32, at 150 it's 6.5 heading 28, and at 30 it's 4.1 heading 50. The ratio from 30 to 100 gives an exponent near 0.34, while the ratio from 100 to 150 gives about 0.12, so the estimates are noisy and I need to combine them somehow.

I'm fitting the shear exponent with a log-log least squares over the three heights, which gives roughly 0.3 even though the noise is about 0.5 m/s. For the veer, the directions at 30 and 150 imply about -18 degrees per unit, and the 100 m reading pulls the base direction to roughly 35. Drag clearly matters, since the fall from 100 m takes 7.13 s against 4.52 s in vacuum, so I'm planning to compare a few drag values against the data.

I'm estimating the drag coefficient at around 0.027, a bit below 0.03, by scaling the dt1 change from the 0.03 to 0.05 range. The sensitivity may not be linear, so I'm checking whether it shifts near the lower end. I'm also starting on the dt2 estimate from the 2.04 over 0.02 ratio.

I'm checking the impact positions next, treating the along-heading offsets as the part that drag affects. In each test the predicted displacement falls short of the measured one, which fits with drag being set too high. The cross-track offsets look like they come from wind instead.

I'm checking the fit: test 2 is off by about 2.2 along track and 0.9 across, which is mostly noise, so the drag estimate of roughly 0.027 seems reasonable. Next I need to account for the updraft, since every operational drop has to fall through the smoke column near the fire centre. I want a calibration drop that lands at the origin, and I also need to look at how the wind changes with altitude, because the hotspot constraints depend on it.

I'm going to run three smoke drops at different altitudes, with the release points backed out from the earlier test displacements so they should land near the fire centre. That separates the updraft effect from the wind at each height.

I'm deciding to run smoke drops at 60 and 125 metres instead of repeating altitudes, since different heights will separate the shear and veer better. For the 60 m drop I'd need a release offset from a simulation, which is affordable. I'll do two now: one replicating test 1 from (-20.2, -106), and one replicating test 2 from (-119, -43.3).

Fall times come out noticeably longer in both cases, and the updraft looks strong while the impact shift stays modest. Next I'm reading the wind numbers at the three heights, averaging the readings at 100 and 150 meters, and estimating the shear between the levels.

I'm fitting the wind veer with the shear estimates from the three heights, which gives a rough slope of about -17 and leaves the numbers a bit noisy. Next I'll test how the updraft guesses of 5 and 10 change the result, using a wind of 5.9 at direction 34.

I'm estimating the updraft from the two data points: the slope between 5 and 10 gives about 5.67, and the second pair gives about 5.64. The curve looks convex, so I'll settle near 5.6 and try that. The wind parameter residuals on tests 1–3 are small, though test 3 is off by 1.8 in y, while tests 4 and 5 pass.

I'm checking how the tests 4 and 5 pass through the smoke at low velocity near the ground, then comparing the result at 5.6.

I'm estimating the updraft at roughly 5.8 m/s, so I'll try 5.85 next. Test 4 overshot north by about 3.3, while test 5 undershot east by 2.2, which doesn't line up along-track. Wind could account for the north offset in test 4 as well.

I'm now weighing whether the low-altitude wind is pushing too far north, since test 3 and test 4 both show north offsets in the slow fall. That points toward stronger shear or an eastward veer near the ground. Next I'm planning more test drops at 45, 60, and 125 m, through the smoke, to pin down the wind at other altitudes before refitting.

I'm settling on a plan for the remaining drops: one inside the smoke at 60 m heading west, and two outside it at 125 m and 45 m, released from far corners so they land well clear of the origin.

I'm going through the wind readings at each height, with speeds and directions at 30, 45, 60, 100, 125 and 150 meters. The directions sit around 50 degrees down low, drop to about 34.5 at 100 meters, then 27 at 125 and 27.5 at 150. I'm going to fit a linear trend of direction against height, anchored at 100 meters.

I'm working through a linear fit of wind direction against height, centered on 100 meters, with the slope coming out to about -22 and the intercept near 36. The low-altitude readings all sit around 50 degrees, which doesn't sit well with a straight line, but I'll keep the linear model for now. I'm also starting to set up a log-log relationship between height and speed.

Now I'm working out the log-log fit of speed against height, computing the deviations from the means for each point.

I'm checking the speed fit's slope and intercept, which come out to a shear of about 0.24 and a wind speed of roughly 5.8. I'm now comparing a working hypothesis against these numbers: a drag of 0.027, wind speed 5.8, direction 36, shear 0.24, veer -22, and an updraft of 5.8.

I'm checking the residuals against the expected noise, which works out to a mean miss of about 1.88. Test 8 is showing a small dx of 3.4 that I'm breaking down along the track direction to see whether it's undershooting.

I'm working through the remaining residuals: test 7 undershoots along-track by about 2.2, test 2 overshoots slightly, and test 5 is short by 1.2. The fast drops seem to fall short, which points to drag being a bit low. The time deltas also run slightly negative, so I'm considering whether the cross-track offsets at the higher altitudes reflect a wind direction or magnitude that's off.

I'm considering whether a coordinate-wise sensitivity sweep is worth the remaining budget, since the hotspot drops are scored on distance and even 1-2 m of model error costs a fair amount per hotspot. I'm also thinking the last two test drops should probe low-altitude slow and high-speed conditions, since the hotspot updrafts will differ in strength.

I'm going to use the two remaining test drops now to gather more data, choosing conditions that differ from the earlier ones, like a lower altitude with a different heading and speed, and a higher-altitude run at a southwest heading.

The second drop at heading 200 and speed 50 from 130 m only covered about 33 m, so drag must be slowing it fast, with the wind pushing it northeast. That puts the release point inside the smoke column from the start, which is still useful for learning about the updraft. Now I'm setting up test 9, releasing from (-63.4, -61.6) at heading 45, altitude 35, speed 75.

I'm also noting that test 10 repeats the second drop, starting from the release point inside the smoke column at heading 200, speed 50, altitude 130. I'm also wondering whether the test drops should be kept for later use, since they won't serve any purpose once the operation begins, so I'll use them.

I've confirmed the test drops are back to zero, so the earlier double-count is gone. Next I'm adding two new wind points to the dataset and refitting the direction model on all ten points, starting by checking the mean of the x-values.

Still computing the direction model's sums and slope across the ten points...

Still working through the regression sums and the speed model's slope, and I'm now comparing the updated values for drag, wind speed, direction, shear, veer and updraft against the earlier ones.

I'm checking test 10, where the predicted fall is too short by about 0.26 and the position errors are around 2.9 and 2.2, and it seems to linger in smoke near the axis. A stronger updraft would lengthen the fall, but tests 4 and 5 show much smaller time errors, so I'll try an updraft of 6.0 and see how it behaves. I'm also considering a more systematic route: computing the sensitivities of the outputs to each parameter.

I'm going to fit the parameters by least squares, but doing that by hand over 30 residuals with 6 parameters is heavy. A coordinate-wise approach may be easier. First I'll measure how the outputs respond to each parameter by perturbing drag, wind speed, wind direction, shear, veer, and updraft one at a time.

I'm computing the Jacobian columns by working out how each step changes the residual, starting from the base residual r0. I've got the per-step vectors for T1 through T6, and I'm partway into T7.

Filling in the Jacobian columns for the drag, wind-speed, and wind-direction perturbations across steps T8 through T10.

Filling in the shear-perturbation column for each step, checking the values against the base residual.

Still filling in the Jacobian columns for the veer and up perturbations...

Checking the up-perturbation column for the later steps, where the updraft change pushes T10's dt residual from -0.26 toward zero.

I'm checking which combination of perturbations would fix the two non-smoke tests, T7 and T8, which both have large positive x residuals. For T7 the residual points mostly along the reverse heading, so it's undershooting along track by about 2.8. For T8 I'm splitting the residual into along-track and cross-track parts, and the cross-track part is the larger one.

I'm weighing whether this is really a fitting problem or just noise: the mean miss of 1.91 is about what pure noise would give, so further fitting may only buy a modest improvement. Still, systematic parameter errors would carry into the hotspot predictions, so I'm considering a least-squares setup with dt weighted more heavily.

Setting up the least-squares system now, with the six parameters as unknowns and the dt residuals scaled up.

I'm writing out the residual rows for the least-squares system, matching each test's x, y, and dt components against the drag, wind, shear, veer, and updraft columns.

Still filling in the least-squares rows, now for the y-components and the dt rows of the remaining steps.

Still filling in the least-squares rows, now for the remaining tests' x, y, and dt components.

Now I'm writing out the last rows of the least-squares system, covering the y and dt components for tests 9 and 10 as well as their wind, shear, veer, and updraft entries.

I'm adding the wind measurements in as a prior, since they already gave estimates for wind speed, direction, shear, and veer with some uncertainty, and I'm working out what standard deviation each one implies in step units.

I'm setting up the normal equations for just the drag and updraft parameters, holding the others fixed for now. I'll compute the sums of the drag and updraft sensitivities and their products with the base residuals, then check the result against the wind priors.

Computing the per-test entries for the drag and updraft columns now, pairing each residual with its sensitivities and accumulating the products.

Now I'm going through the normal-equation sums for the drag and updraft columns, test by test, multiplying each sensitivity by its residual.

Now I'm summing the squared drag sensitivities and the products with the residuals across the tests, which gives the running total for the drag column.

Summing the drag and updraft products across all the tests, I'm getting a running total of about -39 for the cross terms.

Now I'm summing the squared updraft sensitivities, where the larger values come from the T5 and T10 dt rows, and running that total alongside the drag column.

Now I'm finishing the sums for the updraft column, pairing each updraft sensitivity with its residual and its drag counterpart.

Now I'm working out the drag-and-updraft column sums from the per-step products, landing on a total of about -98 for the updraft residual term. With the normal-equation matrix filled in, I'm setting up the determinant to solve for the two parameters.

Working through the numbers, the solve gives a drag change of about -0.0002 and an updraft change of about +0.3, and I'm checking the T10 dt residual with those values, which lands around -0.09 seconds. Next I'll run the same check on the T4 dt row.

Now I'm moving to the full six-parameter least-squares setup, including all the wind columns alongside drag and updraft. I'll write out each row's sensitivities before accum

I'm working through the remaining sensitivity terms, R17 through R20, and getting their products. Then I'm adding them into the running sum, which is currently being carried through each step.

Still summing the sensitivity terms...

Now I'm setting up the linear system for the unknowns, with the matrix rows and right-hand side values filled in.

Now I'm solving the linear system by Gauss-Seidel iteration, starting from the current guesses for a and f.

Now I'm checking the remaining terms of the Gauss-Seidel pass, with the updated values for c and d feeding into e and a.

Now I'm working through the Gauss-Seidel update for b, which comes out to about -0.187 after the second pass, and I'm starting on c.

Now I'm iterating the Gauss-Seidel update for d, which comes out to about 0.278 after the second pass, and I'm starting on e from the new value of c.

Now I'm finishing the Gauss-Seidel update for a and f, getting a around -0.109 and starting to work out f from the latest values.

Now I'm rechecking the d update in the third pass, with b now around -0.18 and f at 0.626.

Now I'm rechecking the Gauss-Seidel values for a, d, and f in the third pass, and they've settled near a≈-0.12, b≈-0.18, c≈-0.10, d≈0.29, e≈-0.095, f≈0.635. Next I'm translating the drag, ws, wd, and shear figures.

I'm noting the veer and updraft adjustments, which come out to -19.95 and 6.12. Now I'm setting those against the hypothesis to see whether they fit.
The miss is down to 1.72 and the step size is 0.044, which is close enough to the noise floor that I don't need to tune further. I'll start the run now.

I'm settling on mid-range values and leaning toward the lowest altitude, since that seems to cut uncertainty overall. Speed should also be low, because along-track error from drag grows with speed. So I'm trying a first set at heading 342, altitude 107, speed 49, and now I'm moving on to a second option with heading 54 and altitude 93.

I'm working through the remaining test cases, setting heading, altitude, and speed for each and estimating the release point from the along-track and wind-drift displacement. I'm going to refine those release estimates by simulating and correcting the offset.

I'm running through the remaining test cases, working out a release point for each from its along-track and wind-drift displacement. Then I'll simulate all five.

I'm working through the corrections, comparing each target against its current position to find the offsets to apply.

I'm finishing the offset list, checking the last few targets against their current positions, and then noting that the smoke nonlinearity needs a re-simulation.
I'm refining the corrections for T2, T3 and T4, since their offsets are much larger than T1 and T5, which are only 0.3 off and fine. Next I'll re-simulate those three.
All the targets are within about 0.8 m now, so the remaining offset on T3, roughly (−0.6, −0.6), is small enough to skip. I'll apply the fine adjustment of (1159.4, −963.5) and drop it now.
